10340-dab-kinzer-a-story-of-a-growing-bo:
William O. Stoddard published this boys' story in 1884, following Dab Kinzer on a Long Island farm and coast. Dab starts with a new suit and a wedding, then meets city boys, pigs, boats, and a railway train in a string of comic mishaps. The book treats boyhood as a mix of work, play, and growing sense.

Crabs, a boat wreck, a rescue, fishing, fog, and a cruise in the Swallow fill later chapters. Dab learns to tell one kind of boy from another, and to stand his ground. Readers get a cheerful, old-fashioned tale of farm life, seaside fun, and a boy becoming steady and kind.
10724-the-store-boy:
Horatio Alger Jr. wrote The Store Boy in his familiar rags-to-respectability manner, following Ben Barclay, a country lad on the road. The story opens as Ben, driving a horse, meets a hard-looking tramp who begs a ride to Pentonville. Ben hesitates, wary of so rough a traveling companion, before the journey begins.

From that meeting, Alger builds a tale of work, honesty, and pluck, as Ben seeks a place in a store and proves his worth. The novel belongs to Alger's long run of boys' books that sold by the million. Young readers get adventure with a moral, in the style that made Alger's name a byword for rising by merit.
12493-how-john-became-a-man-life-story-o:
Isabel C. Byrum's little volume tells the true life story of John, a motherless boy, as a moral lesson for young readers. Her preface hopes the book will show boys the wrong in evil habits. It quotes that a people are destroyed for lack of knowledge, and trusts John's earnest prayer that his story may help others escape snares.

John's path runs from temptation and harmful habit toward prayer, discipline and manhood, told in simple, earnest prose. Illustrations, including one captioned Learning to Pray, reinforce the lesson. The book belongs to early twentieth-century uplift literature for boys, direct in aim and plain in style, valuing character over adventure.
12633-a-happy-boy:
Bjørnstjerne Bjørnson's Happy Boy, translated from the Norse by Rasmus B. Anderson in an author's edition, was written in 1859 and 1860. Anderson, designated by Bjørnson as his American translator, cooperated with the author, who revised each work before translation, giving personal attention to the edition.

A preface calls the tale Bjørnson's best story of peasant life, praising distinct characters, profound psychological insight, artless simplicity and thorough sympathy with hero and surroundings. Popular throughout Scandinavia, the story follows a Norwegian farm boy toward happiness through work, love and faith. The book offers a gentle, classic tale of rural Norway, in a translation the author himself approved.
14533-hocken-and-hunken-a-tale-of-troy:
Arthur Thomas Quiller-Couch, writing as Q, set this Cornish tale in Troy, a small port town of sailors, barbers, and farmers. Captain Cai Hocken hauls ashore to open the story.

Cai and his friend 'Bias, both elderly bachelors, fall for the widow Mrs. Bosenna, and their rivalry runs through regattas, parlour games, letters, auctions, and a final jubilee. Quiller-Couch writes in warm dialect and gentle comedy. The novel is a charming tale of late love in a Cornish town, full of boats, gossip, and second chances. Q's Troy stories were beloved by Cornish readers.
16682-adrien-leroy:
Charles Garvice wrote this London tale of clubs, dinners, and high society, issued by George Newnes in London. It opens on a cold spring night in the West End, where shops shut, tired workers head home, and rich folk in taxis speed west for dinner. Two men in evening dress wait at a Pall Mall club for Standon and Leroy.

Garvice sets rich life against work life in the first pages, then lets love and social games take over. The tale moves through clubs, drawing rooms, and late dinners, with talk as its main engine. Readers who like old society novels will find a smooth, talky romance of London's smart set and the hearts caught in it.
16867-the-adventures-of-odysseus-and-the:
Padraic Colum wrote this 1918 retelling of Odysseus and the tale of Troy, issued by Macmillan in New York with pictures by Willy Pogany. Colum dedicated it to Hughie and Peter, whose imaginations rise to deeds and wonders. Part one follows Telemachus seeking his father and hearing the tale of Troy from Menelaus and Helen. Part two follows Odysseus leaving Calypso's isle, meeting the Phaeacians, and telling of Cyclopes, Scylla, and Charybdis.

Colum retells Homer in clear, storyteller prose for young readers, keeping wonder and peril in fair share. His book has stayed a favorite first Odyssey, reprinted many times through the 1920s. Young readers get a grand, readable voyage home, best read before tackling Homer's epic in full.
16990-the-story-of-troy:
M. Clarke wrote this 1897 school book on the story of Troy. The American Book Company issued it in New York, Cincinnati, and Chicago. A head of Homer from the British Museum serves as frontispiece. Contents run from Homer, father of poetry, and the gods into Troy before the siege. The judgment of Paris, the league against Troy, and the wrath of Achilles follow. The death of Hector and the fall of Troy come next. The Greek chiefs after the war close the book.

Clarke retells the Iliad in plain, schoolroom prose, with chapters that track the war year by year. The book gives young readers a clear first Troy, without the full epic's weight. It still serves as a friendly introduction to Homer's tale, best read before tackling the Iliad itself.
18646-gypsy-s-cousin-joy:
Elizabeth Stuart Phelps wrote this Gypsy book, reissued at New York in 1895 by Dodd, Mead and Company, with a new preface by the author. Gypsy is a lively tomboy in short dresses and long stockings who paddles rafts, climbs trees, skates, and tramps, usually muddy and a little torn. Phelps, who wrote the tales when hardly more than a girl herself, marvels in the preface that Gypsy is now thirty years old in print.

This volume brings cousin Joy into Gypsy's circle, with chapters on news, chestnuts, a discovery, a night's story, and a climb up Rattlesnake. Fun, health, hope, truth, and kindness mark the heroine throughout. The book remains a cheerful classic of girls' fiction from the 1800s.
1948-the-story-of-a-bad-boy:
Thomas Bailey Aldrich's Story of a Bad Boy follows Tom Bailey, a boy sent from New Orleans to live with his grandfather in Rivermouth, New Hampshire, and to attend school there. Tom's badness is of the mild, boyish kind: pranks, scrapes, and adventures with his friends, told by Tom himself in later years.

The book is often called the first American boys' novel. Its charm lies in its realism: a boy who is neither saint nor villain, in a town drawn from Aldrich's own childhood. Readers who know Tom Sawyer will see the debt, and readers new to Aldrich will find a sunny, funny introduction to a New England boyhood.
19751-the-mayor-of-troy:
Arthur Thomas Quiller-Couch wrote this comic novel of Troy, a Cornish borough, published in the early nineteen hundreds and dedicated to Kenneth Grahame and the crew of a small ship. A major, a mayor, a millennium, and a battle of gallants and diehards drive the fun.

Chapters run from a Guernsey merchant's meddling to a bomb, a farewell to Albion, and a merry-go-round close, with the major learning that no man is necessary. Quiller-Couch's Troy books blend Cornish local life with high-spirited farce. Later chapters stage the battle of Talland Cove, where Gunner Sobey takes his turn.
19999-the-drummer-boy:
Mary Anna Phinney's The Drummer Boy is a story of the Civil War. In 1861 the Manly family gathers in their little sitting room. A question of the most serious importance faces them all. It concerns Frank in particular, the drummer boy of the title. Frank's mother sits by the table, pretending to sew. The family's debate is whether a boy shall march to war. Drummer boys were the army's youngest soldiers.

Thousands of boys under eighteen served as drummers and musicians. Their stories filled Northern magazines during and after the war. Phinney writes Frank's choice with a mother's-eye sympathy. The sitting-room scene weighs duty against a child's safety. Such tales taught young readers the war's cost at home. This one is tender, patriotic period fiction.
20492-terry-or-she-ought-to-have-been-a-:
Terry, or She Ought to Have Been a Boy is a story about a girl with a boy's name and a boy's spirit. A servant in the house speaks her mind about the christening. Except for that, she tells the mother, the child was born all right.

When you put a man's name on her, the woman says, something got into the poor lamb. That something will take a good while to work out of her. The tale follows Terry's scrapes and high spirits, and it lets readers judge whether a tomboy's ways are a fault at all.
21371-our-soldier-boy:
A British merchant family in Portugal leaves its eight-year-old son with the servants for a few minutes. They are unaware how close the Peninsular War fighting has come. French troops attack, kill the servants, and leave the child with a bad head wound. A corporal of the Fusiliers later finds him while scouting the villa for food.

George Manville Fenn makes the boy the regiment's mascot, raised by the corporal and his wife, with no memory of his real parents. In time he heroically rescues the colonel himself in battle. Months later the Portuguese give a ball for the British victory, and among the guests are the Trevors, whose name belongs to his lost life.
21626-adrift-in-the-wilds-or-the-adventu:
A steamer runs up the California coast at the start of Edward S. Ellis's Adrift in the Wilds, copyrighted in 1887. She is a day's sail from San Francisco, and passengers pack for landing. A money panic back east has ruined Brandon, Herman and Company, driving the tale's start.

Two boys are shipwrecked on the wild shore, far from the golden gate. Tim, their Irish companion, spies Indigenous folk with a cry for heaven to preserve them. A tiny canoe drawn from hiding gives the party a chance. Ellis, a giant of the dime novel, packs peril into every chapter.
21812-paul-gerrard-the-cabin-boy:
Paul Gerrard goes to sea as a cabin boy in this tale by W. H. G. Kingston, a master of boys' sea stories. Paul's father has lost his estates in a legal fight with the Devereux family, and the sea offers the boy a living. To his surprise, a young Devereux serves in the same midshipmen's mess. Paul saves the wounded man's life, and wary dislike slowly turns to friendship.

The tale opens in a Channel gale, with a fine frigate fighting out to open ocean. Kingston fills his pages with swimming, sharks, wrecks, battles, and pirates in his true style. The editor of this edition calls it a cracking audiobook. Young readers get honor, danger, and forgiveness at sea.
22407-the-adventures-of-piang-the-moro-j:
Florence Partello Stuart wrote The Adventures of Piang, the Moro Jungle Boy, in 1917. Piang is a boy of the Moro people in the Philippines. Stuart wrote after finding Americans ignorant of their own colonies.

The general impression, she says, was that Manila was the Philippines. Few knew the group holds several thousand little islands. Each island harbors its distinct tribe, dialect, and religion. Stuart aimed her boy's adventures against that ignorance. Piang's jungle life introduces young readers to Moro country. The book mixes adventure with geography and custom. It shows how American children's books taught empire through one boy's story.
22497-cab-and-caboose-the-story-of-a-rai:
Kirk Munroe wrote Cab and Caboose, the story of a railroad boy. Munroe wrote adventure books that aimed to teach as they thrilled. A later framing note praises wholesome reading for boys' leisure hours.

Boy Scout leaders, that note says, learned a boy must be influenced wisely. His out-of-door life alone would not shape him fully. The diversions of his other leisure moments mattered just as much. Good stories were part of that shaping by design. Within the tale, a boy learns railroading from cab to caboose. Munroe fills the run with signals, yards, and danger. Readers get period railroad life through a young worker's training.
22944-the-history-of-little-peter-the-sh:
Old Betsy walks half a mile each day in The History of Little Peter, the Ship-Boy. She had known Mary Gray from childhood and came daily, without fee or reward, to help during the long illness from which Mary suffered. Peter, meanwhile, spent his days out on the downs, minding Farmer Ashton's flock of sheep.

From such humble beginnings the tale sends its boy toward the sea promised by the title. Peter's story follows the pattern of the improving children's book, hardship, kindness, and reward in steady sequence. The village scenes ground the adventure in real poverty and real charity. Readers meet a vanished England of downs, farms, and sickrooms, drawn by a writer who expected young readers to feel, as well as follow, the plot.
23375-jack-at-sea-all-work-and-no-play-m:
George Manville Fenn wrote this sea tale about Jack, a clever, bookish boy who takes little sport or exercise. His father, Sir John, and the family doctor fret over it. They decide the cure is a voyage. Sir John buys a yacht fit to sail round the world, and the whole party sets off, with Ned, a servant from home, aboard.

Crew, sails, strange ports, and scrapes at sea fill the pages, as Jack learns the world outside his books. The copy used here lacks two pages and part of two more, torn or lost, but the tale runs clear around those gaps. Fenn makes the moral light and the fun broad, showing how work, play, and sea air can turn a dull boy into a livelier one.
23771-the-hoosier-school-boy:
Edward Eggleston published The Hoosier School-Boy in 1883, a school story of Indiana boyhood. Its hero, Jack, arrives as the new scholar and soon earns his place among boys with nicknames like King Milkmaid and Little Christopher Columbus. The frontispiece warns, Not there, not there, my child.

Chapters bring a battle, hat-ball and bull-pen, pigeon pot-pie, and an exploring expedition. Jack defends his friends, chases a fox, and faces being called to account, with a foot-race for money and a spelling lesson along the way. Eggleston, who knew the Hoosier schoolroom from life, writes its rough fun and rough justice with warmth.
24013-the-telegraph-boy:
Horatio Alger Jr. published The Telegraph Boy as the completion of his sketches of street life in New York, begun eleven years earlier with Ragged Dick. Alger dedicates it to three young friends, Lorin and Beatrice Bernheimer and Florine Arnold, and writes with pride of the public's warm reception.

The telegraph boy class, he notes, came into existence only a few years before, yet its boys are already so numerous that scarcely a downtown ride lacks one for a fellow passenger. Most live with parents in comfortable homes, but a few, like his hero, do not. Alger urges readers to help such waifs through the Children's Aid Society, whose wise plans for its young wards had already met abundant success.
24251-left-behind-or-ten-days-a-newsboy:
James Otis, author of Toby Tyler, Mr. Stubbs's Brother, and Raising the Pearl, wrote this boys' book, published by Harper and Brothers in New York as part of Harper's Young People Series, at a dollar a volume. The series beside it offered Captain Polly, Uncle Peter's Trust, Dorymates, The Flamingo Feather, Wakulla, The Ice Queen, and Otis's own Silent Pete and Tim and Tip.

The title gives the plot in brief: a boy left behind spends ten days as a newsboy, learning to fend for himself on city streets. A picture shows a woman feeding him patiently, on page one hundred and twenty. Readers get a plain, kind-hearted story of a boy's short spell of independence, told for young readers.
24663-the-rich-little-poor-boy:
Eleanor Gates, author of The Poor Little Rich Girl, wrote this novel, published at New York and London in 1922. Its chapters are named for a wicked giant, pride and penalty, a feast and an excursion, four millionaires, new friends, and a dearest wish. A picture shows what the boy saw holding him spellbound in his chair.

Gates reverses her earlier tale: here a poor boy finds himself among riches, and must learn what wealth can and cannot give. Her story mixes fantasy, humour, and feeling, with a child's eye for wonder. Young readers get a charming novel about money, wishes, and the things that matter more.
25486-david-the-shepherd-boy:
Amy Steedman retells the boyhood of David for young readers, in Thomas Nelson's Bible story series. David, youngest son of Jesse of Bethlehem, watches his father's flocks on the hillside while seven big brothers do men's work at home. Bethlehem lies off the beaten track, reached by a steep road through olive groves and sheepfields. The boy's days pass among sheep, with only the hills for company.

David's faith proves itself when lion and bear threaten the flock, and he tells Saul that the God who saved him from paw and claws will save him from the Philistine. Saul offers royal armour and sword, but David refuses them, untrained in their use. He takes his shepherd's coat and sling, the only weapon he thoroughly understands. The book pairs David with Joseph the Dreamer and other childhood Bible tales.
26075-the-erie-train-boy:
Horatio Alger Jr.'s 1891 novel follows Fred, a boy working the Erie road, after his father's death leaves his mother and him with far less than they expected. Mr. Ferguson, cold and brief, tells Fred his father failed to insure his life, and the boy must make his own way.

Chapters mix train adventures with a missing valise, a false suspicion that lands Fred in prison, a trap for Mr. Palmer, and calls on Mr. Ferguson and Ruth Patton. Fred falls under suspicion, clears it, and ends a newspaper hero, with Rose Wainwright's party and a run of good luck closing the tale. The book is a straight Alger story of pluck rewarded.
26104-that-scholarship-boy:
Emma Leslie's school story follows the new boy at Torrington's, whose arrival stirs the whole school. Leonard and his sister Duffy puzzle over the stranger's name, while Taylor and his popular party scorn the newcomers as beggars setting themselves up as gentlemen. A quiet combination of students answers the bullying.

The combination's class answers soon show its meaning, and angry Taylor finds the plan backed by parents taken into confidence. Chapters move from brother and sister talk through Dr. Morrison, a champion's stand, and a righteous retribution, ending with news for Mrs. Morrison. The tale rewards pluck, fair play, and loyalty to schoolmates under pressure.
26255-sonny-boy:
Sophie Swett's 1904 children's book follows Sonny Boy Plummer and his six brothers and sisters. It opens with a dinner-table letter from Aunt Kate, the right kind of aunt who never forgets a birthday. Sonny Boy soon goes on a journey, makes friends, and hunts for his white mice, whose loss drives much of the fun.

Later chapters bring a crookeder boy, school days, and a question over who shall be captain of the company. Pictures show Aunt Kate's summons, a coachman clearing the way with his fists, and a boy named Otto at his one good time. Sonny Boy's gift of his mice to Otto mixes joy with grief, and the book praises kindness in a child's plain, warm voice.
27235-the-voyage-alone-in-the-yawl-rob-r:
John MacGregor's The Voyage Alone in the Yawl Rob Roy, sixth edition of 1893 from Sampson Low, logs a lone sail. It runs from London to Paris and by Havre across the Channel to the Isle of Wight. MacGregor, captain of the Royal Canoe Club, cooked and slept on board without any companion.

Fine weather came along the dangerous coast of France, and an amphibious interlude carried the yawl inland to the Paris Exhibition. Across the broad Channel, one hundred miles to Cowes and its regattas, rough water and dark nights of thunder gave way to bright skies on the Thames and Medway.
27666-seek-and-find-or-the-adventures-of:
Oliver Optic, the pen name of William T. Adams, published this boys' story with Lee and Shepard of Boston, entered in 1867 and copyrighted in 1895. It ran third among the serial stories in Our Boys and Girls, as the sequel to Breaking Away.

Optic dedicates the book to his young friend Alice Lee Gookin, and thanks the young friends who wrote hundreds of letters, with generous commendation and an occasional criticism. His hero, Ernest Thornton, is a smart boy, perhaps too smart. His smartness is no worldly cunning, but the stuff of a noble and true man. An illustration shows Ernest swimming for the despatch barrel.
29333-war-letters-of-a-public-school-boy:
Paul Jones, lieutenant of the Tank Corps, wrote the war letters collected in this volume, published by Cassell and Company in 1918 with eight plates. Jones was scholar-elect of Balliol College, Oxford, and leader of the modern side and football captain at Dulwich College in 1914. His father Harry Jones supplies a memoir, calling him the embodiment of the best public-school spirit.

Part one follows Jones from childhood through Dulwich, football, cricket, and editing The Alleynian. Part two prints his war letters, and part three closes the book. A plate shows Rupert Brooke among the illustrations. Readers get a young officer's war in his own words, framed by a father's grief, from the generation that went from school to the trenches.
296-the-cash-boy:
Frank Fowler, a cash boy, learns he is not his mother's son at all. Horatio Alger Jr.'s Cash Boy opens with a conspiracy that stole a baby from his kin and gave him to a kind woman. Mrs. Fowler raises Frank beside her daughter Grace without favor.

At her death Frank learns the truth, and a kind neighbor shelters Grace while Frank sets out to earn his way. Hardship follows, but kindness to an old man reveals his relatives and true name. Alger's moral of honest work carries the tale. The book shows his rags-to-respect formula.
29828-is-he-popenjoy:
Anthony Trollope published Is He Popenjoy? in London in 1879, in a third edition from Chapman and Hall. Life at Manor Cross and the deanery opens the tale, with Lord and Lady George, Miss Mildmay, and Jack de Baron among the early figures. News from Italy, bad tidings, and a visit to Cross Hall gate stir the plot. Then comes the question of chapter fourteen: are we to call him Popenjoy?

The marquis comes home, sees his brother, and moves among his friends, while the claim of the boy from Italy hangs over all. Trollope treats the matter with his usual dry wit and social care. The book is a tale of rank, marriage, and inheritance, where one name can decide a family's fate and fortune.
30463-john-whopper-the-newsboy:
John Whopper, a Boston newsboy, tells tall tales of travel in a book published in 1871 and entered for copyright in 1870. Pictures show his air-line route to China and his visit to the North Pole. He starts one Tuesday morning, very early, carrying a large bundle of papers from Roxbury toward Jamaica Plain.

Hoping to save time, he cuts across rough, barren fields and jumps a fence at a spot he will not name precisely. After about a third of a mile, his shortcut turns strange, and the story launches into comic voyages. Whopper narrates with cheerful exaggeration, turning an ordinary paper round into a globe-spanning joke for young readers.
30567-the-bondboy:
George W. Ogden writes The Bondboy, published in Chicago in October 1922 by A. C. McClurg, following his earlier Trails End, Claim Number One, The Land of Last Chance, and The Rustler of Wind River. Nineteen chapters open with delivered into bondage, a dry-salt man, the spark in the clod, and a stranger at the gate.

Later scenes add the secret of the clover, blood, deliverance, will he tell, and the sealed envelope. Let him hang, Peter's son, the sunbeam on the wall, until the day break, and deserted follow, with the state versus Newbolt near the close. Ogden tells a story of bondage, debt, and a boy's fight for freedom in the American West.
3127-being-a-boy:
Warner calls being a boy one of the best things in the world. It needs no experience, though it takes some practice to be a good one. Its fault is brevity: just as a boy grows used to the state, he must become something else, with far more work and not half so much fun. Yet every boy longs to be a man and chafes at the limits placed on him.

The chapters that follow remember that restless age in detail. Yoking up teams, roaming fields, and dodging chores fill the pages. The book charms because Warner writes as one who has kept the boy's view intact: work is real, play is serious, and growing up looks both welcome and unfair at once.
32246-adventures-and-reminiscences-of-a-:
George T. Ulmer's Adventures and Reminiscences of a Volunteer, or A Drummer Boy from Maine, was entered in 1892. Ulmer served in Company H, Eighth Maine Volunteers, and dedicated the book to the Grand Army of the Republic. Ulmer's preface warns readers plainly. He does not attempt a history of the rebellion, nor assume correctness in dates to a day. He writes with no aim of posing as a hero, since his deeds fell far short of heroism.

Ulmer holds that the war's true heroes mostly died in it. Perhaps writing the book may stamp him a hero, for whose audacity someone may kill him. He intends instead to dress his little work in homely, rugged, everyday language, striving not for literary merit but for a truthful account. Readers get a Civil War drummer boy's memoir, modest, direct, and deliberately unheroic, from a Maine volunteer.
3229-helen-of-troy:
Andrew Lang retells the story of Helen in this 1882 poem, published by George Bell and Sons in London. The Chiswick Press printed it, and an Old French epigraph sets a tone of courtly sorrow before the verse begins. Lang, scholar of myth and ballad, takes the most famous face in Greek story as his subject.

The poem follows Helen from Sparta's court to Troy's walls, weighing beauty, blame, and fate as the old poets weighed them. Lang writes with a classicist's care, in verse that favors music over novelty. Readers who know the Iliad will find a Victorian retelling: respectful of its sources, tender toward its heroine, and aware that no retelling can settle whether Helen chose or was chosen.
33465-little-miss-joy:
Emma Marshall's Little Miss Joy, in a new edition from London in 1892, follows a girl whose story opens with waiting and watching. Its frontispiece shows Patience telling Joy that she has often wished she had known her mother, a tender scene that sets the book's tone. Marshall, author of Little Queenie and Blue Bell, writes for young readers with warmth and moral care.

The tale's charm lies in its gentle, domestic pathos, as Joy learns of her mother and finds her place in a loving home. Its chapters move from waiting to joy itself, with a novelist's eye for a child's heart. For readers who enjoy Victorian girls' books, Little Miss Joy offers a sweet, old-fashioned story of loss, love, and home.
33544-carrots-just-a-little-boy:
Mrs. Molesworth, writing as Ennis Graham, tells the story of a small boy nicknamed Carrots in this 1876 children's book, illustrated by Walter Crane. Thirteen chapters follow Carrots from his sister Floss's baby through his sixth year, his plans, a lost half-sovereign, trouble and recovery, a long-ago story, a bewitched tongue. A little dog named Gip shares his adventures.

Molesworth writes with warmth and humor about a real child's misunderstandings, kindness, and growing sense of right. The book, dedicated to six little cousins, belongs to the best Victorian tradition of family stories, where small domestic events matter greatly. Young readers and adults reading aloud will enjoy its gentle comedy and affectionate tone.
3785-in-the-reign-of-terror-the-adventur:
George Alfred Henty sends a Westminster schoolboy to France on the eve of the Revolution in this boys' tale. The boy's family debates the journey, weighing a long road among a people in upheaval. Soon he is caught in the Terror itself, with mad dogs, demon wolves, and gathering clouds as early warnings. Chapters carry him through the September massacres, the arrest of Marie, the shadow of Robespierre, and the drownings at Nantes.

Henty promises facts kept correct where the story needs them, save for the Nantes dates, which he owns he moved. The hero's courage lies in protecting friends rather than in battles, and the escape to England closes the book. Young readers who like history with adventure will find a brisk and stirring introduction to revolutionary France.
479-little-lord-fauntleroy:
Frances Hodgson Burnett tells of Cedric Errol, a kind American boy who learns he is heir to an English earldom, in this beloved children's novel. Cedric lives in New York with his widowed mother, loved by shopkeepers and friends. When his stern grandfather summons him to England, Cedric's goodness begins to melt the old earl's pride.

Burnett writes with warmth and gentle humor, letting a child's plain kindness shame adult greed. Velvet suits and curls made Fauntleroy a fashion craze in his day. The book endures as a sweet tale of innocence softening rank, and of a boy who stays himself in a castle.
5111-the-real-diary-of-a-real-boy:
Henry A. Shute's book presents itself as a boy's diary, found years later in a salt-box fitted with leather hinges in his father's shed chamber. The entries record school, pranks, friendships, and small-town life with the spelling, boasts. Earnestness marks every entry, and a later introduction looks back on them thirty years on.

The diary's humour lies in its honesty: the writer takes himself very seriously while the reader sees the comedy. It offers a warm, funny portrait of American boyhood around the turn of the century. It has lasted as a small classic of humour precisely because its hero never knows how funny he is.
5778-try-and-trust-or-abner-holden-s-bou:
Horatio Alger tells the story of Abner Holden's bound boy in Try and Trust, opening around a breakfast table. Benjamin Stanton tells his wife he had a letter from Ohio the day before, from his sister Margaret, who moved there with her husband ten years earlier. From that domestic opening, the novel follows a bound boy's struggle for fair treatment, honest work, and a chance to rise.

Readers meet Alger's familiar pattern with fresh feeling: a young hero, hard masters, kind friends, and steady effort rewarded. The book favors clear morals and brisk incident over fine psychology, which is its charm for young readers. It offers a plain, encouraging tale of trust earned and kept, in the world of farms, shops, and small-town bargains.
658-the-fall-of-troy:
Quintus Smyrnaeus, a Greek poet of Smyrna from about the fourth century, continues Homer's tale in this epic, here in A. S. Way's 1913 translation. The Iliad ends with Hector's burial; Quintus takes up the story from Penthesileia, queen of the Amazons, through Memnon, Achilles' death, the arms of Achilles, the Wooden Horse, and Troy's sack.

Way's verse keeps Homer's ring and music in English, with notes on the Cyclic poets whose works are lost. Fourteen books carry the war to its fiery end. The poem serves as the great sequel to the Iliad, where a later Greek poet completes what Homer left unsung.
9257-the-three-golden-apples-from-a-wond:
Hawthorne's Three Golden Apples, from A Wonder-Book, opens by the Tanglewood fireside after a snowstorm. The storm lasted a day, then cleared in the night, and morning sun shone on bleak Berkshire hills. Frost-work covered the windowpanes, till children scratched peepholes with their nails to glimpse the world outside.

Then comes the tale of Hercules and the golden apples, told for young listeners in Hawthorne's easy style. The frame and tale together make a cozy winter evening. The story remains a favorite retelling of Greek heroism for children, warm and clear.
9331-the-hunted-outlaw-or-donald-morriso:
Published without an author's name, this true tale tells of Donald Morrison, the Canadian Rob Roy, a hunted outlaw. Its prologue mocks psychology, which maps the soul into neat territories of feeling, yet stands stunned when a respected, educated, happy man commits a crime no one foresaw. Truth, it says, is stranger than fiction.

Morrison, high in position and without enemies, became a fugitive all the same. The book follows his flight and the hunt for him across Canada. It remains a vivid outlaw narrative, part crime report and part folk legend, from the days of the frontier.
9383-moni-the-goat-boy:
Johanna Spyri, author of Heidi, wrote this Swiss tale of Moni the goat-boy, translated by Helen Dole. It opens with a long, steep climb to the Bath House at Fideris, up through the Prättigau valley. Horses pant so hard that travelers dismount and clamber on foot to the green summit. In the flock's midst comes the goat-boy himself.

Chapters tell of Moni's mountain life, a visit, a time when he can no longer sing, and a time when he sings again. Charles Copeland's color pictures grace the book. It remains a gentle Alpine classic, simple, musical, and full of mountain air.
a-happy-boy: Bjornstjerne Bjornson tells of a happy boy in this story of Norwegian peasant life. Written in 1859 and 1860, it is judged the author's best peasant tale by its translator. Bjornson draws characters with distinctness, psychological insight, and artless simplicity. The story follows a boy's growth in a farming community. The tale is warm, simple, and true to farm life in Norway.
adrien-leroy: Charles Garvice writes Adrien Leroy, published at London by George Newnes Limited, opening on a cold night in early spring with the West End streets nearly deserted. Great shutters are drawn down with a dull rumble and the pavements grow dreary as the plate-glass glories are hidden. Tired workers with haggard faces make their way homeward. Taxis and smart motors speed westward toward dinner, and two men in immaculate evening dress wait outside a luxurious Pall Mall club.
being-a-boy:
Charles Dudley Warner remembers his Connecticut farm boyhood in this book of sketches, and the first chapter states his case outright. One of the best things in the world to be is a boy, he writes; it needs no experience, only practice, and its one defect is that it does not last. His proudest day was driving the oxen alone, with a load of apples, to the cider mill.

Warner rebuilds the farm year from a boy's height. Driving cattle with the long whip, teaching his cows Latin, sugaring, fishing, and the long tyranny of chores and school fill the chapters. He corrects his younger self as he goes, regretting the lash he once laid on patient oxen. It is a memoir of a lost rural world, written before it had quite vanished.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-amoy:
Amoy was a Catholic mission district in China, created in 1883 and placed in the care of the Dominican order. Its territory took in the island of Formosa with nearby small islands, among a native population the article puts near four and a half million, about two million of them on Formosa.

Catholics numbered under four thousand, with just over a thousand on Formosa, served by eleven European and eight Chinese priests. The district counted thirty-two churches or chapels, three orphanages, and thirteen schools teaching 242 pupils, a small Catholic presence inside a very large population.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bl-marie-chri: Blessed Marie Christine of Savoy, daughter of Victor Emmanuel I of Sardinia, was born at Cagliari in 1812 and died at Naples in 1836. Her father died in 1824 and her mother in 1832. Charles Albert pressed her to court at Turin. There she wed Ferdinand II of the Two Sicilies in November 1832. She died at twenty-three, fifteen days after bearing her son Francesco, Duke of Calabria, famed for her virtues.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-blessed-marga:
Margaret of Savoy, Marchioness of Montferrat, left court life after widowhood to found a Dominican monastery at Alba. Born at Pignerol in 1382, she was the sole daughter of Louis of Savoy, Prince of Achaia. She married Theodore of Montferrat in 1403 and was widowed in 1418.

Moved by the preaching of Vincent Ferrer, she handed the marquisate to her stepson. She joined the Third Order of Saint Dominic. She refused a second marriage to Philip Maria of Milan, even against a papal request to release her vow. With young women of rank she founded the Alba monastery, lived in deep mortification, and died in 1464.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-boniface-of-s:
Boniface of Savoy, forty-sixth Archbishop of Canterbury, reached the primacy through his sister Beatrice, mother of Queen Eleanor. A Carthusian from childhood, he became Bishop of Belley in 1234 and administered Valence in 1241. After two popes died in quick succession, Innocent IV confirmed his Canterbury election late in 1243.

He found his see deep in debt and cut sinecures and needless offices to pay it down. Consecrated at Lyons on 15 January 1245, he won seven years of first-fruits from vacant benefices and a province-wide levy. Enthroned with great pomp on All Saints' Day 1249, he met fierce resistance when he extended his visitation to suffragan dioceses. He excommunicated the clergy of Saint Paul's and felled the sub-prior of Saint Bartholomew's. He died in Savoy on 14 July 1270.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-claude-franco:
Claude-Francois-Dorothee de Jouffroy, Marquis d'Abbans, a mechanician born at Abbans near Besancon on 30 September 1751 and dead at Paris on 18 July 1832. Quingey's Dominicans educated him, but he leaned toward mechanics. He joined the Bourbon infantry at twenty. He was confined in 1772 opposite Cannes. There he began studying steam navigation.

To Paris he went in 1775 to study the Watt engine and debated Perier. An experimental boat on the Doubs in 1776 used web-foot paddles and failed. In 1781, promised government help, he built the pyroscaphe at Lyons. It measured 140 feet long and 150 tons, its engine driving paddle wheels. On 15 July 1783 it ran up the Saone against the current at six miles an hour before thousands of spectators. It worked the river for sixteen months. The Academy withheld endorsement and the promised monopoly failed. After the Revolution and Fulton's success, a Seine boat of 1816 won him a patent.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francis-mollo:
Francis Molloy, called O'Molloy, was an Irish Franciscan theologian and grammarian born in King's County at the start of the seventeenth century and dead at St. Isidore's, Rome, about 1684. He entered the Franciscan order young and lectured in philosophy at Klosterneuburg near Vienna in 1642. He moved to the theology chair at Gratz in 1645, and there published a Scotist book on the Incarnation. About 1650 he was called to Rome as primary professor of theology at St. Isidore's College.

In Rome he wrote theological works and a long Latin poem on Prince Prosper Philip of Spain. He is best known for two Irish books from the Propaganda press: the Lucerna Fidelium of 1676, an Irish catechism in Irish language and characters dedicated to Cardinal Altieri. The Grammatica Latino-Hibernica of 1677, the first printed Latin-Irish grammar, was dedicated to Cardinal Massimi.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francois-duqu:
Francois Duquesnoy, also called Francois Flamand and in Italy Il Fiammingo, was born at Brussels in 1594 and died at Leghorn on 12 July 1646, a Flemish sculptor of Louis XIII's age. Son of an excellent Dutch sculptor who taught him first, he carved Justice on the Brussels chancellery portal and two angels for the Jesuit church while young. In 1619, at twenty-five, Archduke Albert sent him to Rome, where he lived many years and made works of importance.

To him Rome owes the handsome baldachin over the high altar of St. Peter's, the colossal St. Andrew with his cross also in St. Peter's, and the Santa Susanna in Santa Maria di Loreto, while Ghent Cathedral holds his rococo tomb for Bishop Triest. He is famous for sporting children in marble and bronze and ivory drinking cups, and Brussels's Manneken is commonly attributed to him.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-georges-darbo:
Georges Darboy, Archbishop of Paris from 1863, was shot by the Commune in May 1871 blessing his executioners. Born near Langres in 1813 and ordained in 1836, he taught at Langres seminary, joined Affre at Paris in 1845, and rose to canon of Notre-Dame and vicar-general. As Bishop of Nancy from 1859 he founded the Saint Leopold school, enlarged the seminary, and wrote his 1862 letter on the need of study.

Promoted to Paris in January 1863, Darboy consecrated the restored Notre-Dame basilica within a year and served as grand almoner, senator, and imperial councillor. His Gallican deference to the empire and his stand at the Vatican Council, where he joined the minority deeming infallibility's definition inopportune, marked his tenure, though he later subscribed to it. Arrested on April 4, 1871, and held at Mazas, he was shot at Roquette on May 24. A national funeral followed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gerald-molloy:
Gerald Molloy, an Irish theologian and scientist born near Dublin in 1834, proved a priest could lead in science. Schooled at Castleknock and Maynooth, where theology and physical science both shone, he became Maynooth's theology professor at twenty-three in 1857. He held the chair until 1874, then moved to Ireland's Catholic University to teach natural philosophy. In 1883 he succeeded Dean Neville as rector, serving until his death.

Molloy sat on manual-training commissions, the Royal University's senate, and its governing board, ending as vice-chancellor. For the Royal Dublin Society he lectured on natural science, above all electricity, once debating lightning conductors with Oliver Lodge. His Geology and Revelation of 1870 reconciled geology with revealed religion, and Gleanings in Science of 1888 gathered popular lectures. He died suddenly at Aberdeen in 1906, days after receiving an honorary law doctorate there.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-baptiste:
Jean-Baptiste Carnoy, a Belgian priest and biologist born in 1836 near Tournai and dead in Switzerland in 1899, built Louvain's school of cell study almost from nothing. Ordained after seminary at Tournai, he turned to natural science, earned a science doctorate, and worked in Germany with Hanstein at Bonn and in Leipzig, Berlin, and Vienna.

Recalled to Belgium, Carnoy at last got his Louvain post in 1876, starting with practical microscopy. His manual of microscopy and his work on fungi and cells trained a generation, and his journal gave Belgian biology a home. Pastoral posts at Celles and Bauffe had slowed him, but Louvain let his talent for patient, exact observation bear full fruit.

Jean-Baptiste de Belloy, cardinal archbishop of Paris, was born in 1709 at Morangles and died in Paris in 1808, just short of a hundred. Of an old military family, he chose the Church, studied at Paris, and took a theology doctorate in 1737. Kindness and steady faith marked his ministry more than book learning.

Belloy became bishop of Glandèves in 1751 and later of Marseilles, where quarrels over the bull Unigenitus threatened schism. By tact and fairness he won both sides and restored peace. When revolution suppressed his see in 1790 he protested and withdrew, yet lived to guide Paris through Napoleon's years with the same gentle firmness.

Jean-Baptiste-Julien d'Omalius Halloy, a Belgian geologist born at Liège in 1783 and died at Brussels in 1875, surveyed France on foot before he governed provinces. Sent to Paris in 1801, he caught a love of natural history from Buffon and attended lectures by Cuvier and others, turning home journeys into field trips.

Charged with mapping the empire, he walked over fifteen thousand miles through France and parts of Italy by 1813, though his family pressed him to quit. His map, printed in 1822, grounded the finer surveys of Dufrénoy and Élie de Beaumont. After serving at Dinant and Liège, he governed Namur from 1815 until after the 1830 revolution.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-de-jouff:
Jean de Jouffroy, a French prelate and statesman born about 1412 at Luxeuil and dead in 1473. He studied at Dôle, Cologne, and Pavia, joined the Benedictines, and lectured at Pavia on divinity and church law. Philip the Good of Burgundy sent him on missions across France, Italy, Portugal, and Spain.

He was abbot of Luxeuil and bishop of Arras, and became a favourite of the dauphin, later Louis XI, and sought the cardinal's hat through Burgundy's help. As papal legate in 1461 he pressed Louis to repeal the Pragmatic Sanction of Bourges, which had curbed Rome's sway in France. The king agreed in words, while quietly seeking Naples gains Rome would not grant.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-thomas-t:
John Thomas Troy was the Dominican Archbishop of Dublin who governed through the Whiteboy troubles and the age of revolution. Born near Dublin in 1739 to Anglo-Norman stock, he joined the Dominicans at Rome, studied philosophy and theology, became prior of St. Clement's in 1772, and was appointed Bishop of Ossory in 1776 over the diocese's own nominee, arriving at Kilkenny that August.

For nine years he labored for his diocese in troubled times, sternly denouncing the Whiteboys, secret bands of farmers who attacked landlords and tithe-proctors at night. His Roman upbringing left him unsympathetic to the miseries driving them, and his bent toward authority made him unpopular, though he zealously corrected abuses and promoted education. Rome recognized his worth by making him administrator of Armagh in 1781, and he later became Archbishop of Dublin, dying there in 1823.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-brumoy:
Pierre Brumoy was a French Jesuit humanist, born at Rouen in 1688. He joined the Society in 1704 and belonged to the distinguished humanist circle that honoured the order shortly before its suppression in France. Between 1722 and 1739 he wrote many articles for the celebrated Journal de Trévoux, editing it for a time. He also completed volumes eleven and twelve of the History of the Gallican Church, covering 1226 to 1320.

He also wrote college tragedies on sacred subjects, poems and discourses in Latin and French, and a Latin didactic poem on the passions, De motibus animi, highly esteemed by contemporaries. His chief work, Le théâtre des Grecs, published in 1730 in three volumes, translates and analyses Greek tragedies with keen critical and aesthetic notes, and was often reprinted. Charlotte Lennox, aided by the Earl of Cork and Samuel Johnson, translated it into English in 1759. He died at Paris in 1742.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-savoy:
Savoy, French Savoie and Italian Savoja, is a district in south-eastern France from Lake Geneva to south of the Arc river, now the departments of Savoie and Haute-Savoie. The House of Savoy, now ruling Italy, takes its name from this land. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia follows Celts, Burgundians, and counts across fifteen centuries.

Roman Sabaudia was home to the Celtic Allobroges, conquered by Rome in the first century before Christ and slowly Romanised. When Huns destroyed the Burgundian kingdom at Worms in 437, killing King Gundikar, the survivors settled in Sabaudia with Roman general Aëtius' leave under Gundiok. After Rome fell they built a kingdom over the Rhône basin to the Cévennes and the sea, until Savoy joined the Frankish realm in 532.
doe-osti-2589834-additive-manufacturing-: Iron alloys for reactors got 3D-printed, and this DOE report covers additive manufacturing. The pages detail the nuclear environment testing. The reactor materials folks get their data. The alloys were Fe-based. The testing was nuclear environment. The folks were reactor material.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-HargravesRoy_Ha: Harold Weisberg wrote on November 14, 1990 to a man named Dave, whose surname is illegible, about visitors to the Assassination Archives and Research Center. The center drew researchers who came to work in its files in person. Weisberg's letter reports on that traffic. The surviving record gives the date and subject but no details, so it stands as late correspondence from the archive's circle.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-Playboy_Playboy: An issue of Playboy magazine is preserved here for two of its contents. One is a history feature by James McKinley. The other is 'The Missing Oswalds,' about the Kennedy assassination. Playboy published serious journalism beside its photographs, and the Oswald piece belonged to that side of the magazine. The file gives the two features and the magazine. It does not give the issue's date, so the piece's argument cannot be dated or summarized further.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-TrulyRoy_Truly_: Roy Truly ran the Texas School Book Depository, the building from which shots were fired at President Kennedy. His digest gathers his account of Lee Harvey Oswald, who worked for him, drawn from his deposition and affidavit. Truly hired Oswald and saw him on the day of the shooting. The digest pulls his scattered statements into one place for readers tracing Oswald's last weeks at work.
helen-of-troy:
Andrew Lang published this long poem with George Bell and Sons in 1882, signing himself A. Lang. A rondeau to all old friends serves as dedication, and the poem is built in books of numbered stanzas. Book I, The Coming of Paris, opens in the palace of Menelaus in Lacedaemon, where a feast is laid and chariots arrive under the trees.

Paris, fairest of mortal men, tells the tale of his past life to his host, the husband he will wrong. Lang follows the old story at epic length: the judgment, the voyage, the carrying off of Helen, and the war that gathers behind her. His stanza is Spenserian, his manner deliberately archaic. The poem is a young scholar-poet's homage to the matter of Troy, written the year before his fame as a folklorist began.
in-the-reign-of-terror-the-adventures-of:
G. A. Henty, the Victorian boys' adventure writer, sent a Westminster schoolboy into revolutionary France in In the Reign of Terror. Harry, a scholar whose reports always read fair, leaves school for a post with a French noble family. His father judges the French freedoms hopeful rather than dangerous. Henty warns his readers that the tale, not history lessons, comes first.

Clouds gather as the Revolution turns from reform to violence in Paris. Chapters follow a mad dog attack, a demon wolf, and the September massacres of 1792. Marie, the family's daughter, is arrested, and Robespierre enters the story's path. Nantes and its noyades, the mass drownings of prisoners, mark the Terror's darkest stretch. Harry helps his French friends through prisons, mobs, and flight toward England. Henty packs the history with escapes and loyal service, in his manner: one English lad standing by his friends while a kingdom goes mad.
leo-tolstoy:
Three writers joined in this 1903 study of Leo Tolstoy. G. K. Chesterton treats Tolstoy as a writer. Edward Garnett weighs his place in European literature, and G. H. Perris adds a life note.

Tolstoy still lived when this book appeared in England. The authors argue over his novels, faith, and moral teaching. Chesterton's lively criticism leads the volume's case. A list of illustrations helps readers picture the Russian sage. The book shows Britain discovering Tolstoy as both artist and prophet. Portraits of Tolstoy at work and at home illustrate it. Three voices keep the short book from mere praise.
little-lord-fauntleroy:
Frances Hodgson Burnett opens this novel with young Cedric Errol. Cedric knows nothing of the inheritance awaiting him. His English father died when Cedric was very small. He remembers blue eyes, a mustache, and rides on a shoulder.

Since then, Cedric avoids talking to his mother about him. She returned from illness pale, thin, and dressed in black. Her dimples vanished and her eyes looked large and mournful. Cedric comforts her with kisses learned from his father's pet name. Cedric learned the pet name Dearest from his father's usage. Her arms trembled when the boy asked after his papa.
moni-the-goat-boy:
Johanna Spyri, the author of Heidi, wrote this Alpine tale for children. Helen B. Dole translated it, and Charles Copeland illustrated it in color. The scene is the Prättigau valley in Switzerland, below the Bath House at Fideris. Moni herds goats on the green heights above the village.

Five short chapters tell his story. All is well with Moni, then his life in the mountains, then a visit. A crisis follows: Moni can no longer sing. The last chapter promises that Moni sings again. An illustration shows a boy named Jörgli holding a cross set with many stones, the temptation at the story's heart.
podcast-dannyjones-4eK1mAN05OY:
Neuroscientist Mario Beauregard has argued that mind and brain are not the same thing, a position that cost him standing in his field. With Danny Jones, he tells the story behind the episode's hook: that the Vatican tried to recruit him, and that his exile from mainstream science followed his research on spiritual experience.

Beauregard discusses prayer, near-death states, and the studies he says materialist neuroscience refuses to run. Jones follows the personal thread, how a researcher ends up outside the institutions that trained him. The recruitment claim is Beauregard's own account, kept here as he tells it. Listeners interested in the border between neuroscience and mysticism get a firsthand report from a man who has worked, and been punished, on both sides of it.
podcast-joerogan-YHpbXtDtcoY:
Michael Stevens of VSauce joins the Joe Rogan Experience for episode 528. Stevens built one of the first great science channels on YouTube, asking odd questions and answering them with experiments and delight. Rogan, a fellow professional in curiosity, hosts him warmly.

The two trade the kind of questions Stevens made famous: strange facts about the body, the mind, and the world that reward a second look. Rogan feeds him topics and marvels at the answers. The episode is a light, bright entry in the show's science run, proof that wonder itself can carry a long conversation.
podcast-tuckercarlson-0M5cEOIKfoY:
Airline captain Sherry Walker joins Tucker Carlson to explain a rash of plane crashes. Walker has flown for pay since 1991, nearly thirty-five years. Carlson asks why American air travel feels so much worse.

He notes that tech improved while flying got rougher and riskier. Walker points to a deep corporate shift in the industry. The title promises the real reason behind the crashes. She ties training, hiring, and profit drives to safety loss. The episode speaks to nervous flyers who want a pilot's blunt account. Her years in the cockpit ground every claim.
the-adventures-of-odysseus-and-the-tales: Padraic Colum wrote The Adventures of Odysseus and the Tale of Troy, presented by Willy Pogany and printed by the Macmillan Company of New York with rights held in 1918. Colum gives the book to Hughie and Peter as a telling of the world's greatest story for young minds that rise to deeds and wonders. A long reprint list runs from June 1919 to August 1927.
the-cash-boy:
The Cash Boy, by Horatio Alger, Jr., is announced in its preface as a story about a boy and for boys, and the preface itself gives the whole plot away. The hero was stolen as a baby by conspiracy. He was given to a kind woman who did not know his name. She called him Frank Fowler after her husband. She raised him beside her own daughter Grace, without partiality.

When Mrs. Fowler dies, the truth comes out. The children are left alone, and Frank refuses the poorhouse. A neighbour takes Grace while he starts out to make his way. Kindness to an old man at last reveals his relatives and his right name. Chapter I then opens in Crawford, where the boys are forming a baseball club, the Excelsior Club, to challenge other villages. Alger sells the ending first, then starts the boy at a ball game.
the-fall-of-troy:
Quintus Smyrnaeus, called Quintus of Smyrna, wrote this Greek epic in about the fourth century A.D., and A. S. Way turned it into English in 1913. The poem fills the gap Homer left in the tale of Troy.

The introduction notes that the Iliad covers only some fifty days and ends with Hector's burial. Other bards once told the whole cycle of the war, but their works are lost. Quintus takes up the tale from Hector's funeral to the taking of the city. Readers get the deaths, duels, and dooms that stand between the Iliad and the fall of Troy.
the-hunted-outlaw-or-donald-morrison-the:
An anonymous author tells the story of Donald Morrison. The subtitle bills him as the Canadian Rob Roy. A motto declares that truth is stranger than fiction. The prologue opens away from the outlaw. It attacks psychology as a science of the soul. Psychology strips the soul bare, the writer says. It classifies every emotion with confidence. Its plummet is too short, though. Motive is born in depths it cannot reach.

The argument runs through a familiar puzzle. A respected, educated man commits a startling crime. His home is happy and his name is fair. Every prediction fails at once. Life begins with promise and ends in darkness. An act of a moment mocks all calculations. Heredity, environment, and temperament predict nothing here. That frame presents Morrison's career of flight and pursuit in Quebec. It becomes a case study in unexplained surfaces.
the-mayor-of-troy: Arthur Thomas Quiller-Couch published The Mayor of Troy in 1906. Only the dedication and contents are present here, so the novel itself does not appear. Quiller-Couch dedicated the book to his friend Kenneth Graham and the rest of the crew of the Richard and Emily, with apologies to the mayor of Lostwithiel. The contents promise a prologue, chapters on a major and a mayor, a challenge between Troy gallants and Looe diehards, and a battle of Talland Cove.
the-real-diary-of-a-real-boy:
Henry A. Shute introduces his boyhood diary by recalling a winter search in 1901 and 1902 through an old closet in his father's house. Inside a salt box fitted with leather hinges and a bent-wire catch he found the treasures of his youth.

The inventory mixes fish lines and hooks, a popgun, marbles, a small whalebone bow, and a bean-blower used at school behind a geography book. A frog's leg and a bluejay's wing, both very dry, complete the hoard. Shute's humor lies in treating each trifle as serious evidence, preparing readers for a diary told in a boy's own voice.
the-store-boy:
Horatio Alger Jr., author of Bound to Rise and Phil, the Fiddler, opens this boys' novel with Ben Barclay driving a wagon two miles from Pentonville. A stout, dark tramp with a week's beard and a dirty suit hails him, asking for a ride and claiming to be dead tired.

Ben sizes the man up as a hard-looking tramp and hesitates, but lets him climb onto the seat rather than refuse outright. The unwelcome passenger pulls out a clay pipe. He finds no match. He growls at his luck when Ben has none. The boy is spared the pipe's fumes. He is not spared the long, uneasy ride beside a stranger.
the-story-of-a-bad-boy:
Thomas Bailey Aldrich introduces himself as the bad boy of his own story: not a very bad boy, he insists, but a pretty bad one, and no cherub. He has no dark confessions to make. He offers only the portrait of a friendly, impulsive New England lad. The boy preferred Robinson Crusoe to missionary tracts. He spent his pocket-money royally on peppermint-drops and taffy candy.

Tom Bailey recalls greeting each new scholar at recess by demanding his name, shaking hands cordially with Langdons and Wallaces while treating Higginses and Sprigginses as deadly affronts. His old schoolfellows are now lawyers, merchants, sea-captains, and judges, including little freckled Pepper Whitcomb on the bench, which Aldrich finds wonderful to contemplate.
the-story-of-troy: M. Clarke retells the story of Troy in the Eclectic School Readings series, copyrighted by the American Book Company in 1897. Only the title page and the opening of a contents list appear in this record. An introduction treats Homer as the father of poetry. A chapter on the gods and goddesses follows. The narrative begins with Troy before the siege. The judgment of Paris comes next. The wrath of Achilles and the dream of Agamemnon follow. Clarke's retelling itself does not appear.
the-three-golden-apples-from-a-wonder-bo:
Nathaniel Hawthorne's Three Golden Apples comes from A Wonder-Book for Girls and Boys, framed by the Tanglewood fireside gatherings. The introduction opens after a snowstorm clears over the Berkshire hills. Children at Tanglewood scratch peepholes in the frost-work on the windowpanes and delight in a world whiter than a sheet. Hawthorne declares that bright, hard frost raises the spirits and makes the blood dance like a brook downhill.

After breakfast the whole party, muffled in furs and woollens, flounders out to slide down into the valley a hundred times. Eustace Bright takes three small children on one sledge, hits a hidden stump, and loses little Squash-blossom, who pops red-faced from a snow-bank. This frame introduces the Greek myth of Hercules and the golden apples, retold for children by the fireside storyteller.
try-and-trust-or-abner-holden-s-bound-bo: Horatio Alger Jr.'s Try and Trust, or Abner Holden's Bound Boy, is dedicated to his young friend A. Florian Henriques, called Boisie. The contents open around a breakfast table and introduce the hero in chapter two. Later chapters promise a ghost in the attic, a fraud exposed, Ralph the Ranger, and a four-footed foe. Herbert faces a burglar and is robbed in the night. Only the title page, dedication, and contents are present here, so Herbert's story itself does not appear.
